title: Smoothing the Cliff Edge: MPs on Leaving Parliament
label: 15 September 2026 · Former MPs discuss support after leaving
summary: The Administration Committee heard from four former MPs about their experiences of losing or leaving their seats at the 2024 general election. Witnesses praised the practical support they received but highlighted gaps, especially for staff, and offered suggestions such as clearer guidance, better disposal of equipment, and ongoing career support. They also firmly rejected the idea of returning as buddies for new MPs, stressing that departing MPs themselves need to move on and find work.

chapters.title: Introductions and expectations
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses introduced themselves, and Sir Charles Walker gave a positive assessment of post-election support.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome to this second session of our inquiry into general election planning. We're looking at how former MPs were supported when they left Parliament. Could you introduce yourselves?

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: I'm Nigel Mills; I was MP for Amber Valley from 2010 to 2024.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: I'm Charles Walker, MP for Broxbourne from 2005 to 2024.

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: I'm Thangam Debbonaire, MP for Bristol West from 2015 to 2024.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Sir Charles, you chaired the previous Administration Committee when it worked on this. Did the support after the 2024 election live up to your expectations?

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: Yes, it did. I'd give it nine and a half out of ten. The House service and IPSA performed well, but we always need to improve.

chapters.title: Preparation and unexpected difficulties
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses described how losing their seats was traumatic and that preparation was extremely difficult.

turns.speaker: Bambos Charalambous
turns.text: This is mainly for Nigel and Thangam. How well prepared were you for leaving, and what came as an unexpected difficulty?

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: I expected it—the polls were clear. But you can't really prepare; you can't apply for jobs during a campaign. I rushed to wind everything up in two months, but I'm not sure I'd recommend that.

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: Losing your job is a trauma, especially when it happens on TV in front of everyone. You fight to win, so you can't buff up your CV. I was a 58-year-old unemployed woman making my staff redundant. I did prepare by getting my staff CVs ready secretly, but personally, it was devastating.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We're now joined by Sir Nigel Evans. Nigel, how well prepared were you?

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: I was surprised to lose—my seat had been Tory forever. I hadn't planned. But the support was good; it wasn't the cliff edge it used to be. We had time to sort out offices and housing, and people talked us through pensions and redundancy. It wasn't as brutal as in the past.

chapters.title: Winding up and staff support
chapters.takeaway: The winding-up period was rushed, and staff faced particular difficulties with redundancy and finding new jobs.

turns.speaker: Mary Glindon
turns.text: What was your experience of winding up? Were the deadlines realistic, and did you have support for your staff?

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: The three-month deadline helped. Your pass stops working within days, so you need to be quick. I had prepared my staff, so they got jobs fast. But emotional support is separate from practical help. I paid for private therapy, which made the careers coaching effective. I felt pressure to get staff off the payroll, though that might have been my mood.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: You should plan for your last day on your first day. It's a vocation, not a career. Most people leave because they lose an election. The money runs out long before jobs appear. The House should provide ongoing career development and accredited qualifications. We need to be serious about preparing colleagues to leave.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: The four-month period was confusing. Staff thought they'd get four months' pay, but it's a limit, not a target. I closed my office after two months and paid three. The redundancy process was odd—consultation meetings and letters burned weeks. Staff didn't get the CV and interview support that MPs got. Mine all got jobs, but it was harder for them.

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: I felt guilty about my staff. Getting a P45 at 66 is different from at 36 with a mortgage. Staff don't get the same cushion. When 251 Tories lose, hundreds of staff chase few jobs. They deserve the same support as MPs. We should look after them.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: Also, if staff fear losing their jobs, they may resign before an election, leaving MPs unable to work. A soft landing for staff benefits Parliament too.

chapters.title: Guidance and practical arrangements
chapters.takeaway: Guidance was generally good but could be clearer on staff pay, casework, and equipment disposal.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: How clear was the guidance from the House, IPSA, and parties about winding up?

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: The guidance was mostly good, but there were gaps. A clear toolkit for office managers on data destruction, recycling computers, and handling casework during Dissolution would help. Former constituents still contact me about case notes.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: The guidance was useful. My only gripe was not being able to buy my old printer instead of it going to landfill. Outplacement support was excellent, though.

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: Disposal of kit was annoying. My iPad was taken in a humiliating way, and it just went to a skip. We should be able to buy it.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: The guidance was very good, but the legal side for staff was tricky—notice periods, redundancy pay. A standard pack of letters would reduce errors. IT collection was a bit disorganised, but overall smooth.

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: Richmond House was well organised, sympathetic. The only suggestion I have is to give ex-MPs a standard email like nigel.evans.exmp@parliament.uk so people can still reach us. Losing your parliamentary email is brutal.

chapters.title: Handover to incoming MPs
chapters.takeaway: Casework handover was generally smooth, though some former MPs suggested improvements.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: On handing over to incoming MPs, did casework handover work well?

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: I offered my successor everything she wanted. An ex-MP email would help if she needs to get in touch.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: Most casework was done before polling day. We asked constituents for consent to pass on cases. It wasn't many, and it worked well, though it's not natural to be in touch with your replacement after losing.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: I briefed my successor on a few long-running cases. Most constituents don't realise you cease to be an MP when an election is called. We triaged and asked them to contact the successor.

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: Incoming MPs should assume they start from scratch; any urgent casework will have been dealt with. We provided information on how to contact the new MP. Confidentiality guidance was good, though advice on disposing of confidential waste would have helped.

chapters.title: Balancing support and public perception
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses argued that support for MPs and staff must be balanced against public perception but is necessary to attract good people.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: We need to balance what the public experiences when losing a job with what MPs and staff get. What about employing staff by the House for more security?

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: Why should staff be treated differently? If we want the best, they should get the same support. They face the same sudden loss.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: A good employer supports redundant staff into new jobs. If we don't, we won't attract the brightest to Parliament. Playing to the TaxPayers' Alliance lobby is dangerous. But we should be clear about what we mean on pay.

chapters.title: Rejecting the buddy idea
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses firmly rejected the suggestion that former MPs should return as buddies for new MPs, stressing they need to move on and find work.

turns.speaker: Mary Glindon
turns.text: Would you be willing to return to support new MPs as a buddy?

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: Absolutely not. We've left; new MPs don't want us around. I did many things for free after leaving, but I need to earn a living. If you want better MPs, treat MPs better.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: The last place I wanted to be was here. I emptied my office and left. I'd be no use to a new MP.

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: We were seen as contagious. New MPs should learn the job themselves—go on Bill Committees, ask Doorkeepers. Learn with humility; you will lose eventually. But we need to pay our bills. The answer is no.

chapters.title: Career transition and departing Members' area
chapters.takeaway: Career coaching and emotional support were valuable but should be separate; the departing Members' area was well run but had a sombre atmosphere.

turns.speaker: Bambos Charalambous
turns.text: How prepared were you for work beyond Parliament? Did you use the career transition service, and how important was emotional support?

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: The career transition service was valuable—I thank Charles Walker. It helps translate our skills. I paid for private therapy separately, which made coaching work. I wish the service was offered to staff too.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: Did the departing Members' area work well for you?

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: Yes. It was like speed dating—you move from one desk to another. Well organised.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: It was excellent. Everything was there, sympathetic, well handled.

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: The location felt like a basement while new MPs went to bright rooms. But the service inside was excellent.

chapters.title: Staff outcomes and final thoughts
chapters.takeaway: Most former staff found new jobs, but references and support could be improved; witnesses urged better treatment for staff.

turns.speaker: Bob Blackman
turns.text: Did your successor take on any of your staff, Sir Charles?

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: No. My staff had been with me for years, including my wife. There was no transfer.

turns.speaker: Bob Blackman
turns.text: Are you still in touch with ex-staff, and have they got new jobs?

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: Yes, with all of them. My constituency staff got jobs quickly because we prepared. Parliamentary staff found it harder. I'm a lifelong careers coach for them.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: My staff got jobs. They have transferable skills and don't carry the baggage of having been an MP.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: My staff all had jobs within three months. References were fiddly—IPSA gives basic ones, so I wrote letters on headed paper. It's an awkward situation.

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: One left for the Navy before the election. The others were worried but all found jobs outside the House.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all for your valuable feedback. That concludes this session.
